turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome in. What brings you to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Well, Doctor, I... I came in because things have been getting really out of hand at my apartment building. It's not just a feeling, it's something I've been watching happen day after day. See, I know the people there—my neighbors, the maintenance guys, probably even the people across the hall—they're all watching me. They track my comings and goings. Every time I leave to go to the store, or just step out to get some air, I can feel eyes on me, and I know they're keeping a log or something. And it doesn't stop there. They’ve been slipping these notes about me to the front office. I've seen the papers getting passed around, or stuck to doors. Now, my sister and the building manager, everybody keeps telling me, "Oh, it's just regular notices on the doors, it's just reminders about the trash or the water being shut off." But they don't see what I see. They don't understand that these aren't just regular flyers. It's a whole coordinated thing, and it's exhausting, you know? Just trying to live your life when everyone is keeping tabs on you and reporting back to the office. I just... I can't get anyone to listen to me about what's really going on with these notes.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed, false belief that neighbors and building staff are coordinating to watch them and report on them via notes, despite evidence and reassurances from others to the contrary.

turns.doctor_question: That sounds very stressful to deal with. Have you ever heard voices talking or whispering when no one was physically around you?
turns.patient_response: No, no, I've never had anything like that. I mean, I don't hear voices or whispers or anything spooky like that when I'm alone in my apartment. It's not like that at all. It's the real people, you see? The actual people in the building. I can hear them talking out in the hall, or down in the lobby, and I know they're talking about me. I can hear the murmur of their voices through the door sometimes, just low enough that I can't make out every single word, but I know the tone. I know what they're doing. But it's not like I'm sitting in my living room and hearing voices coming out of the walls or thin air. It's the neighbors, the maintenance man, the people who are actually there, physically there, watching and whispering to each other when they think I'm not paying attention. But I am paying attention. I have to, right? With everything going on, I have to keep my ears open. But no, no invisible voices. Just the real ones, plotting.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed belief that neighbors and building staff are watching, whispering about them, and plotting against them, indicating persecutory and referential delusions.

turns.doctor_question: About how long has this been going on with your neighbors?
turns.patient_response:
Well, let me think on that. It doesn't just start all at once, you know, it sort of creeps up on you. But if I really put a pin in it, to when I first knew for sure what they were doing... it’s been about a year and a month. Yeah, a year and a month. I know that because it was right around the time they sent out those new parking rules last year. I went down to the office to ask about it, and the lady behind the desk gave me this look. Just a real knowing look, like she had a file on me right there under the counter. 

And ever since then, for a whole year and a month, it’s been non-stop. Every time I walk down the hall, every time I take my trash out. You try living like that for over a year, doctor. Thirteen whole months of watching them watch me. It wears a man down, it really does. I mean, I don't work anymore, so I'm home a lot, which means I see it all happen. I see the maintenance guy sweeping the exact same spot in the lobby for twenty minutes just waiting to see when I check my mail. A year and a month of this... it's just too much for one person to handle, but they don't care. They just keep at it, day in and day out, logging everything I do, passing those notes around. Thirteen months of it.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed, false belief that his neighbors and building staff are constantly watching him, keeping a file on him, and logging his activities.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from the stress of this situation, have you been experiencing persistent feelings of sadness, depression, or a loss of interest in things you used to enjoy?
turns.patient_response:
Well... yeah. I mean, it's hard to separate it all out, isn't it? The stress and the sadness, they kind of bleed into each other. But yes, the sadness... it's heavy. It's really heavy. It's not just feeling a little down because of the neighbors, it's... it's deeper than that. 

Most mornings, I wake up with this heavy, hollow feeling in my chest. It's like... like the day already went bad before I even get my feet on the floor. I open my eyes, and there's just this immediate weight pressing down on me, telling me there's no point in getting up. And I used to like doing things, you know? I used to like tinkering with old radios, fixing them up. I had a whole workbench set up in the corner of my living room. I'd spend hours just fiddling with the dials and the wires, getting the static just right. But now... I look at that workbench and I feel absolutely nothing. The dust is just piling up on it. I haven't touched a radio in months. I just sit in my chair, staring at the wall, feeling that hollow ache. It's like all the color has been drained out of everything. 

And it's not just the radios, it's everything. I don't even care about watching my shows anymore. I used to watch the history channel every night, but now the TV just stays off. It's too much effort to even pick up the remote. I just sit there, feeling so empty, so incredibly sad, and it just doesn't lift. It stays with me all day, no matter what I do. It's like carrying a sack of wet sand around with me everywhere I go in that apartment. And when you combine that with knowing everyone is watching you... it's just... it's a lot, doctor. It really is.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient mentions 'knowing everyone is watching you,' indicating a persecutory or referential delusion.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient describes a persistent, heavy, hollow feeling of sadness and emptiness that stays with them all day.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient explicitly states they no longer care about or engage in previously enjoyed activities, like tinkering with radios or watching TV.

turns.doctor_question: Before this deep sadness began fourteen months ago, had you ever felt that people were watching you or plotting against you?
turns.patient_response:
Well, the neighbors... that’s a whole different story, doctor. It’s not just tied up with this heavy, wet sand feeling that’s been crushing me for the last fourteen months. Even before I got completely stuck in my chair, long before the gray fog got this thick, I knew what they were doing out there. Living in an apartment building like mine, you get to know the sounds of the place, and you know when things aren't right. 

Actually, I remember there was this one spell, just a few weeks, where the fog actually lifted a little bit. I was actually eating a bit better—maybe fixing a real sandwich instead of just forcing down dry toast—and I wasn't waking up feeling quite so completely hopeless every single morning. I thought to myself, "Maybe I'm getting my energy back. Maybe I can finally get back to my workbench and look at those radios." 

But even then... even when the sadness backed off for a minute and I had a little bit of strength, I still knew they were out there. I still believed the neighbors were watching my door and reporting on me. I'd hear the floorboards creak out in the hall, or I'd see a shadow pass under the gap at the bottom of the doorframe, and I just knew they were keeping a log of everything I did. When my lights went on, when I ran the water, if I even walked near the peephole... they were keeping track. I don't know exactly who they report to—the landlord, maybe someone else, I really couldn't tell you—but it never stopped. It makes you feel like a prisoner in your own home, it really does. You try to just mind your own business, but you can feel their eyes on you right through the wood. So, yes, long before the deep sadness took over, and even during the times I felt a little bit of relief from the heavy feeling, the watching... the watching never stopped.
